headline: Principal AI Product Manager | B2B Vertical SaaS · Construction · Insurance · Legal | GenAI & Agentic Products | 0→1 Launch Specialist
about:
I have been building AI products since before the GenAI boom and have learned that great AI products start with deep empathy for the customer problem and understanding how to apply this powerful technology to solve them.

Over the past 6 years I have led zero-to-one AI launches across three vertical SaaS companies in construction, and insurance The pattern I keep finding is that the industries most underserved by technology have the most to gain from AI, and the least patience for products that don't work on day one. This is what shapes how I build. My focus is turning AI into real customer impact. 

I have shipped Procore Assist (the largest GenAI product in construction tech, 10x customer base in 2.5 months), CrunchAI for Specifications (50%+ customer adoption in 2 months), and Agentic Underwriting at Federato. Each one started with deep customer empathy and ended with a measurable business outcome.

I am a Principal AI PM who specializes in vertical SaaS for underserved industries. If you are building AI products for construction, insurance, legal, or similarly complex B2B markets, let's talk. 

My product principles:
🧐 Customer Curiosity: Get close to customers, understand their world and uncover what others miss.
🎷 Collaboration+Creativity: Product teams are a jazz band. I set the rhythm, but the whole team improvises to create amazing music.
🚀 GTM Impact: I focus on building what moves the customer and the business.

I am passionate about the craft of product management and contribute via community building and coaching. I co-host the ATX Product Happy Hour in Austin. I formerly published a newsletter Austin Voice of Product. I coach and mentor aspiring and growing product managers especially women to develop the next generation of product leaders.

publications.title: Does Infrastructure Investment Lead to Economic Growth or Economic Fragility? Evidence from China
publications.publishedAt: Oxford Review of Economic Policy 32(3):360-390 · September 2016 DOI: 10.1093/oxrep/grw022 · Sep 1, 2016
publications.description: China’s three-decade infrastructure investment boom shows few signs of abating. Is China’s economic growth a consequence of its purposeful investment? Is China a prodigy in delivering infrastructure from which rich democracies could learn? The prevalent view in economics literature and policies derived from it is that a high level of infrastructure investment is a precursor to economic growth. China is especially held up as a model to emulate. Politicians in rich democracies display awe and envy of the scale of infrastructure Chinese leaders are able to build. Based on the largest dataset of its kind, this paper punctures the twin myths that (i) infrastructure creates economic value, and that (ii) China has a distinct advantage in its delivery. Far from being an engine of economic growth, the typical infrastructure investment fails to deliver a positive risk-adjusted return. Moreover, China’s track record in delivering infrastructure is no better than that of rich democracies. Investing in unproductive projects results initially in a boom, as long as construction is ongoing, followed by a bust, when forecasted benefits fail to materialize and projects therefore become a drag on the economy. Where investments are debt-financed, overinvesting in unproductive projects results in the build-up of debt, monetary expansion, instability in financial markets, and economic fragility, exactly as we see in China today. We conclude that poorly managed infrastructure investments are a main explanation of surfacing economic and financial problems in China. We predict that, unless China shifts to a lower level of higher-quality infrastructure investments, the country is headed for an infrastructure-led national financial and economic crisis, which is likely also to be a crisis for the international economy. China’s infrastructure investment model is not one to follow for other countries but one to avoid.

publications.title: Big is Fragile: An Attempt at Theorizing Scale
publications.publishedAt: Forthcoming in Bent Flyvbjerg, ed., The Oxford Handbook of Megaproject Management, Oxford University Press · Mar 2, 2016
publications.description:
Abstract:      
In this paper we characterise the propensity of big capital investments to systematically deliver poor outcomes as "fragility," a notion suggested by Nassim Taleb. A thing or system that is easily harmed by randomness is fragile. We argue that, contrary to their appearance, big capital investments break easily — i.e. deliver negative net present value — due to various sources of uncertainty that impact them during their long gestation, implementation, and operation periods. We do not refute the existence of economies of scale and scope. Instead we argue that big capital investments have a disproportionate (non-linear) exposure to uncertainties that deliver poor or negative returns above and beyond their economies of scale and scope. We further argue that to succeed, leaders of capital projects need to carefully consider where scaling pays off and where it does not. To automatically assume that "bigger is better," which is common in megaproject management, is a recipe for failure.

Number of Pages in PDF File: 39

Keywords: Megaprojects, megaproject management, project management, fragility, scaling, economies of scale, cost overruns, schedule overruns, benefit shortfalls, cost-benefit analysis, welfare economics, debt management, large dams, hydroelectricity

publications.title: Banking Sector Restructuring Program in Kazakhstan – BTA Bank JSC
publications.description:
Bank restructuring and sovereign-debt crises continue to be a heated topic of discussion. Greece’s Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras is, for example, openly challenging the deeply unpopular austerity policies underpinning the debt-stricken country’s bailout program. 

Conventional wisdom in international bailout programs tends to favor creditors to the detriment of the sovereign. However, in this teaching case we explore an innovative and successful approach the Government of Kazakhstan took in 2009 to deal with its then impending banking restructuring and sovereign-debt crisis. Zooming in on the case of the BTA Bank of Kazakhstan we explore the following questions: What were the stakes? How did the Kazakh Government manage the competing interests of domestic banks, depositors, international creditors, the sovereign's own solvency, and the tax-payers? Should a government provide direct assistance to ailing banks? What does an effective communication strategy and corporate structure look like in a restructuring crisis?

This case is pertinent today because it is an example of a sovereign taking control of an otherwise potentially crippling financial crisis without imposing outsized penalties on tax payers or on the sovereign. The case study challenges the notion of ‘bowing to international creditors’ and demonstrates that through skilful implementation an issuer can modify market practice and craft solutions suitable to its profile whilst weathering controversy. Kazakhstan provides a framework for Greece and other countries challenged by crippling creditor demands and ineffective austerity programs.

Note: Teaching note available for educators and policymakers.

publications.title: Fluid populations, immobile assets: Synchronizing infrastructure investments with shifting demography.
publications.description: In this article we reconstruct and test conventional economic theory’s deductive claims about the nature of infrastructure assets and the demography of end-users who demand infrastructure outputs. We find that the conventional theory puts forward three mutually reinforcing propositions: that infrastructure assets have a natural tendency towards monopoly owing to technical economies of scale; that infrastructure outputs (such as cubic metres of water or kilowatt–hours of electricity) and end-users of these outputs are essentially homogenous; and that future demand of infrastructure is predictable with a reasonable degree of certainty. These conventional propositions in practice have promulgated a ‘bigger is better’ paradigm in the planning of infrastructure assets and networks that has entrenched the practice of building large immobile infrastructure assets. In contrast, building on evidence from multiple cases – Berlin water authority (Berliner Wasserbetriebe) and World Bank-financed water supply projects in six developing countries – we show that conventional economics theory has led to the development of poor planning practices that are yielding unfavourable outcomes in infrastructure investments. We find that the heterogeneous populations of end-users (individuals, households and organizations) are fluid across space and time. This fluidity makes immobile assets subject to frequent and costly obsolescence. Instead of being theorized as large immobile (and monopoly tending) assets, infrastructure assets should be viewed as modular, plug-and-play, increments. These modules can be flexibly assembled over time to expand or contract capacity in specific places for specific users.

publications.title: Should we build more large dams? The actual costs of hydropower megaproject development
publications.description: A brisk building boom of hydropower mega-dams is underway from China to Brazil. Whether benefits of new dams will outweigh costs remains unresolved despite contentious debates. We investigate this question with the “outside view” or “reference class forecasting” based on literature on decision-making under uncertainty in psychology. We find overwhelming evidence that budgets are systematically biased below actual costs of large hydropower dams — excluding inflation, substantial debt servicing, environmental, and social costs. Using the largest and most reliable reference data of its kind and multilevel statistical techniques applied to large dams for the first time, we were successful in fitting parsimonious models to predict cost and schedule overruns. The outside view suggests that in most countries large hydropower dams will be too costly in absolute terms and take too long to build to deliver a positive risk-adjusted return unless suitable risk management measures outlined in this paper can be affordably provided. Policymakers, particularly in developing countries, are advised to prefer agile energy alternatives that can be built over shorter time horizons to energy megaprojects.

publications.title: Location decisions of large firms: analyzing the procurement of infrastructure services
publications.description: How do large companies buy infrastructure (e.g. electricity, gas or rail)? Mainstream economics literature proposes that in the absence of an intermediating government, the bargaining power of large customers in procuring infrastructure will be weak. Drawing on a spatial, temporal and relational framework, this article critiques this proposition through a case study of a large manufacturing firm, ThyssenKrupp (TK) AG, which recently invested €7 billion in steel processing facilities in Brazil and USA. I find that prior to making durable and immobile investments large firms—like TK—can exert symmetric bargaining power against sellers of infrastructure, provided the firm has competitive alternatives available in making a location decision. TK exerted strong bargaining power by doing extensive analysis; keeping its commitment to any given location alternative low; inducing a ‘relational auction’ among alternatives it found desirable and by demanding tailored infrastructure services, rather than off-the-shelf commodities. Public sector infrastructure megaprojects, built without active co-development with lead users, are likely to be wasteful investments.

Harry made a huge impact during his time as CFO at &Dine, and from the moment he joined, he felt like a fellow co-founder. He brought a blend of commercial acumen, high energy, and deep commitment to our business, treating its challenges and opportunities as his own.

What really stood out was Harry’s ability to build and support a strong team culture. He understood that financial success goes hand in hand with fostering a motivated, high-performing team, and he led by example - always focused on the bigger picture.

Harry is someone who gets things done. He can transform a business and drives it forward. Thanks for everything Harry.

receivedRecommendations.givenByHeadline: Building &Dine: the platform behind how the world’s best companies feed their people
receivedRecommendations.description:
I had the pleasure of working very closely with Harry during his time as CFO at &Dine. From day one, he treated &Dine like his own, bringing passion, energy, and a sharp commercial mindset, along with a great network. During a critical growth phase, Harry played a key role in helping us scale, contributing to a period of 500%+ revenue growth.

His passion and experience with early-stage tech meant he instantly understood both the challenges and opportunities we faced. Beyond just the numbers, he actively helped shape our strategy, improved operations, and strengthened our commercial and fundraising efforts. His ability to bring structure and clarity to our data and reporting was transformative, allowing us to move faster and make smarter decisions.

On top of that, Harry is a great person to work with - he is enthusiastic, collaborative, and always focused on making an impact. Any business looking for a CFO who fully immerses himself in the mission, whilst making the journey enjoyable along the way, would be lucky to have him on their team.

Harry played a key role in &Dine’s growth, overseeing finance during a transformative period where the business scaled revenue over 500% and grew to 15 people. As both an investor and Board advisor, I saw first hand the impact of his work - helping to bring structure and rigour to Board reporting and introducing new data and insights to improve decision-making.

Harry’s real USP is in fundraising and preparing businesses for investment. He understands what investors look for and ensures companies are not only financially sound but also primed for growth. Beyond finance, he’s a commercial thinker who tackles challenges with a strategic mindset.

I continue to mentor Harry. I think he has what it takes to be a successful executive. Any fast-growing business looking for a commercially-minded finance leader who can drive commercial impact and prepare for investment should check him out.

receivedRecommendations.givenByHeadline: Chief Strategy & People Officer @ &Dine | Fractional C-Suite Operator | Scaling marketplaces & Problem Solver | Deliveroo #30
receivedRecommendations.description: I love working with Harry. I really value the way he challenges a business to think and do better. He's diligent and methodical, coupled with strong commercial skills. He thrives on keeping teams alligned and in check, ensuring everyone is accountable for their actions, to drive growth and efficiencies. I'd recommend him to any business as a senior financial leader (CFO) or Chief of Staff. Most of all, he's a top person, who's company is great value and fun to work with.

receivedRecommendations.givenByHeadline: Founder | Marketing Leader 🌟 Follow For Thoughts on Marketing Strategy & More
receivedRecommendations.description: Harry has the ideal combination anyone would look for in a CFO: strategic insight, financial expertise, and a collaborative approach that makes him a great team member. He has a knack for getting to the heart of an issue and asks the right questions to uncover the answers a business truly needs. Intelligent, empathetic, and a natural problem-solver, Harry has a way of bringing out the best in those around him.
